overview.title: A brief history of deep learning frameworks: the three key features and the road to Theano
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.section: 3.1 A brief history of deep learning frameworks
overview.main_topic: Why practitioners use frameworks, the three capabilities every deep learning framework combines, and the early history from the 1964 autodiff paper through CUDA to Theano
overview.central_idea: All deep learning frameworks (Keras, JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch) combine three features: automatic differentiation, tensor computation on CPUs/GPUs/specialized hardware, and distribution across devices and machines. These ideas are old (automatic differentiation dates to 1964), but robust reusable packages came only after Python's rise, NVIDIA's CUDA (2006) and Theano (circa 2009), the conceptual ancestor of all modern tools.
overview.importance: The three-feature list is a compact definition of what a framework is for, and it explains what Keras delegates to its backends. The history explains why the ecosystem looks the way it does.
learning_objectives: Name the four frameworks the book teaches and state which is the oldest.
List the three key features all deep learning frameworks combine.
Explain how neural networks were built before frameworks: hand-written gradients in C++ and no practical GPU programming.
Describe the late-2000s developments (Python's rise, CUDA in 2006, CUDA-based networks from 2009, Theano circa 2009) that made frameworks possible.
prerequisites: Automatic differentiation with tf.GradientTape in the from-scratch example (p.80)

summary:
Section 3.1 opens by noting that in the real world you will not write low-level code from scratch as at the end of chapter 2; you will use a **framework**. Besides Keras, the main ones today are **JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch**, and the book teaches all four.

These frameworks are recent, with **Keras the oldest (launched March 2015)**, but the ideas behind them are old: the first paper on **automatic differentiation** was published in 1964 (Wengert, *Communications of the ACM*, footnote 1). All frameworks combine **three key features**:

1. computing gradients of arbitrary differentiable functions (**automatic differentiation**);
2. running tensor computations on **CPUs and GPUs** (and possibly other specialized hardware);
3. **distributing** computation across multiple devices or computers (several GPUs in one machine, or GPUs across separate machines).

"Together, these three simple features unlock all modern deep learning."

The history: from the 1960s until the 2000s, autodiff had **no practical application in machine learning**; people working on neural networks wrote their own gradient logic by hand, usually in C++, and GPU programming was "all but impossible." In the late 2000s things changed: **Python** and its ecosystem gained ground over MATLAB and C++ in science, and **NVIDIA released CUDA in 2006**, enabling neural networks on consumer GPUs. CUDA initially targeted physics simulation, but from **2009** ML researchers built CUDA-based networks, typically one-off, single-GPU, without autodiff.

The first framework combining autodiff and GPU computation for training deep models was **Theano, circa 2009**, "the conceptual ancestor of all modern deep learning tools." It gained traction in research in **2013-2014**, after the **ImageNet 2012** results ignited interest in deep learning. Around then, other GPU-enabled libraries were becoming popular in computer vision (the sentence continues on p.86 with Torch 7 and Caffe).

paragraphs.what_it_says: In practice you will use a framework rather than low-level code from scratch; besides Keras the main frameworks are JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch, and the book covers all four.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The from-scratch MNIST exercise of section 2.5 was for understanding, not for practice. Even it relied on a framework for the hardest part, gradient computation (tf.GradientTape, p.80).

paragraphs.what_it_says: The frameworks are all quite recent, Keras being the oldest (March 2015), but their ideas are old: the first paper on automatic differentiation dates from 1964. All frameworks combine three key features.
paragraphs.what_it_means: There is a roughly fifty-year gap between the theory (Wengert's 1964 program for evaluating derivatives automatically) and its mass use in deep learning tools. The bottleneck was not ideas but hardware, language ecosystems and engineering.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It reframes frameworks as packaged engineering of known ideas, and introduces the list that defines what a framework must provide.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Wengert's 1964 paper described what is now called forward-mode automatic differentiation; deep learning frameworks mainly use reverse mode, which is what backpropagation is.

terminology.meaning: Computing exact derivatives of a program by applying the chain rule to its elementary operations, as opposed to symbolic or numerical (finite-difference) differentiation.

connections: p.80: tf.GradientTape records operations to compute gradients automatically

paragraphs.excerpt: A way to compute gradients for arbitrary differentiable functions (automatic differentiation)
paragraphs.what_it_says: Feature 1: computing gradients for arbitrary differentiable functions, i.e. automatic differentiation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: You write the forward computation (model plus loss) and the framework gives you the gradient with respect to any inputs or variables, which is what made the backpropagation of chapter 2 something you never implement by hand.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Without it, every new architecture or loss would require deriving and coding gradients manually, as the page says people did before the 2000s.
paragraphs.technical_idea: 'Arbitrary' means any composition of supported differentiable operations, including control flow such as loops and conditionals in eager frameworks.
connections: p.83: backpropagation is possible because all tensor operations are differentiable

paragraphs.excerpt: A way to run tensor computations on CPUs and GPUs (and possibly
paragraphs.what_it_says: Feature 2: running tensor computations on CPUs and GPUs, and possibly on other specialized deep learning hardware.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The same tensor code (matmul, relu, ...) must execute efficiently on very different devices. GPUs perform thousands of arithmetic operations in parallel, which suits the large matrix products of neural networks.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Hardware acceleration is what made training deep networks on large datasets feasible; p.86 mentions Google's TPUs and the XLA compiler as one such specialized path.

terminology.meaning: Graphics processing unit; a massively parallel processor well suited to tensor operations.

paragraphs.excerpt: A way to distribute computation across multiple devices or multiple computers, such
paragraphs.what_it_says: Feature 3: distributing computation across multiple devices or computers, such as several GPUs in one machine or GPUs across several machines.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Large models and datasets exceed one device's memory or compute, so frameworks provide ways to split data (data parallelism) or the model (model parallelism) across devices and keep them synchronized.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Distribution is what scales training to the size of modern models; p.86 credits TensorFlow with adding large-scale distributed computation to Theano's ideas.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in data parallelism each device computes gradients on its share of the batch and the gradients are averaged before the update.
connections: p.86: TensorFlow added support for large-scale distributed computation

paragraphs.excerpt: Together, these three simple features unlock all modern deep learning.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Autodiff, hardware acceleration and distribution together unlock all modern deep learning.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Everything else, layers, optimizers and training loops, can be built on top of these three primitives, which is exactly what Keras does on top of its backends.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It provides a checklist for evaluating any framework, present or future.
connections: p.87: Keras needs a backend engine to run

paragraphs.excerpt: It took a long time for the field to develop robust solutions
paragraphs.what_it_says: Solving all three problems robustly and packaging them took a long time. From the 1960s to the 2000s, autodiff had no practical ML use; neural network practitioners wrote gradient logic by hand, usually in C++, and GPU programming was all but impossible.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Before frameworks, changing a model meant re-deriving and re-coding its backward pass, which made experimentation slow and error-prone. The from-scratch example avoided this pain only because it borrowed autodiff (p.80).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why research progress accelerated once frameworks appeared: iteration speed matters as much as ideas.
connections: p.80: the authors note that reimplementing backpropagation for softmax and crossentropy would be cumbersome

paragraphs.what_it_says: In the late 2000s, Python and its ecosystem gained traction over MATLAB and C++ in science, and NVIDIA released CUDA in 2006, making neural networks on consumer GPUs possible. CUDA first targeted physics simulation, but from 2009 ML researchers built CUDA-based networks, usually one-off, single-GPU and without autodiff.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Two of the three ingredients started appearing separately: a convenient high-level language (Python) and general-purpose GPU programming (CUDA). They were not yet combined with autodiff into reusable tools.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows why Python is the language of deep learning today (a point p.86 makes strongly) and why GPUs became the default hardware.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: CUDA is NVIDIA's platform and programming model for running general computations (not just graphics) on its GPUs.

terminology.meaning: NVIDIA's general-purpose GPU computing platform, released in 2006.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Theano, circa 2009, was the first framework enabling both autodiff and GPU computation for training deep learning models; it is the conceptual ancestor of all modern tools and gained traction in 2013-2014 after ImageNet 2012 sparked interest in deep learning. Around then, other GPU-enabled libraries became popular in computer vision.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Theano combined features 1 and 2 in a Python library. The ImageNet 2012 competition (won by a GPU-trained convnet) created demand, and Theano was there to meet it. The sentence about computer-vision libraries continues on p.86 (Torch 7, Caffe), and Keras itself launched in 2015 powered by Theano.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Tracing the lineage (Theano to Keras and TensorFlow) explains shared design ideas across today's frameworks.

concepts.name: Automatic differentiation
concepts.definition: A way to compute gradients for arbitrary differentiable functions, the first of the three key features of every framework.
concepts.intuition: The framework watches the operations you perform and applies the chain rule to them for you.
concepts.technical: Frameworks typically use reverse-mode autodiff (backpropagation), which computes the gradient of a scalar with respect to all parameters at roughly the cost of one forward pass.
concepts.significance: It removed the need to hand-code gradient logic, which practitioners did until the 2000s.
concepts.misconception: Autodiff is not numerical differentiation by finite differences, nor symbolic algebra; it gives exact derivatives of the executed operations.

concepts.name: Deep learning framework
concepts.definition: Software that combines autodiff, tensor computation on CPUs/GPUs/specialized hardware, and distributed computation.
concepts.intuition: The infrastructure layer every model is built on.
concepts.technical: Keras, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch are the four the book covers; Keras is the oldest (March 2015).
concepts.significance: These three features 'unlock all modern deep learning'.
concepts.example: Theano (circa 2009) was the first to combine autodiff and GPU training.
concepts.misconception: Frameworks did not invent their core ideas; autodiff dates to 1964.

concepts.name: GPU computation
concepts.definition: Running tensor operations on graphics processors, made broadly accessible by NVIDIA's CUDA (2006).
concepts.intuition: Thousands of small calculators working in parallel on the entries of a matrix product.
concepts.technical: Researchers implemented CUDA-based neural networks from 2009, initially single-GPU and without autodiff.
concepts.significance: It provided the compute that made deep learning practical.
concepts.example: A (128, 784) by (784, 512) matmul is about 51 million multiply-adds, which a GPU handles in parallel.
concepts.misconception: CUDA was not designed for machine learning; its initial focus was physics simulation.

deeper.title: What 'writing gradient logic by hand' meant
The three features as a building's utilities
deeper.body: Think of a framework as the utilities of a building: autodiff is the plumbing that carries the error signal back to every room, hardware acceleration is the power supply, and distribution is the ability to connect several buildings into one campus. Keras (p.87 uses a house-building image too) is the interior you actually live in.

misconceptions.claim: Deep learning frameworks have been around for decades.
misconceptions.correction: They are all recent; Keras, the oldest of the four, launched in March 2015. Only the underlying ideas (autodiff, 1964) are old.

misconceptions.claim: CUDA was built for deep learning.
misconceptions.correction: Its initial focus was physics simulation; ML researchers adopted it from 2009.

misconceptions.claim: Early GPU neural networks used autodiff.
misconceptions.correction: The CUDA-based implementations from 2009 were typically one-off, single-GPU and had no autodifferentiation; Theano was the first to combine the two.

takeaways: In practice you use a framework; the book covers Keras, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch.
Keras (March 2015) is the oldest of the four; automatic differentiation dates to a 1964 paper.
Every framework combines automatic differentiation, CPU/GPU (and specialized hardware) tensor computation, and distributed computation.
Before frameworks, gradients were hand-coded (usually in C++) and GPU programming was nearly impossible; CUDA arrived in 2006.
Theano (circa 2009) was the first framework with autodiff and GPU training, the ancestor of modern tools, popularized after ImageNet 2012.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three key features the book says all deep learning frameworks combine?
options: Automatic differentiation of arbitrary differentiable functions
Running tensor computations on CPUs and GPUs
Distributing computation across multiple devices or computers
questions.explanation: The three listed features are autodiff, CPU/GPU tensor computation and distribution. Pretrained model collections exist in many ecosystems but are not part of the book's definition.

questions.question: Which of the four frameworks covered in the book is the oldest, and when was it launched?
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of section 3.1.

questions.question: According to the book, which was the first framework to enable both autodifferentiation and GPU computation for training deep learning models?
questions.explanation: Theano, circa 2009, is called the conceptual ancestor of all modern deep learning tools. Caffe was a C++ computer-vision library (p.86), TensorFlow came in late 2015, and CUDA is a GPU programming platform, not a deep learning framework.

questions.question: Automatic differentiation was described in 1964, yet it had no practical ML application until the 2000s. Using the page, explain what else was missing.
questions.answer: Practical GPU programming (CUDA only arrived in 2006), a convenient scientific language ecosystem (Python's rise in the late 2000s), and a reusable package combining autodiff with GPU computation (Theano, circa 2009). Demand also grew only after ImageNet 2012.
questions.explanation: The page emphasizes that the field had to develop robust solutions to all three problems and package them reusably; the idea alone was not enough.

questions.question: How did people working with neural networks compute gradients before frameworks?
questions.answer: They wrote their own gradient logic by hand, usually in a language like C++.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the history paragraph.

questions.question: Why does the third feature (distribution across devices and computers) matter for modern deep learning?
questions.answer: Large models and datasets exceed the memory and compute of one device, so training must be split across several GPUs in one machine or across multiple machines.
questions.explanation: The page lists distribution as one of the three features that unlock modern deep learning; the reasoning about scale is an elaboration beyond the page.

questions.question: Can you place these on a timeline without looking: CUDA, Theano, ImageNet 2012, Keras, the first autodiff paper?
questions.answer: Autodiff paper 1964; CUDA 2006; Theano circa 2009; ImageNet 2012; Keras March 2015.
questions.explanation: All dates are on this page.
